title: 3 Energy Stocks With Dividends Built to Last the Next 10 Years - The Globe and Mail
content: Chevron’s scale and diversification make it an evergreen investment. Brookfield Renewable is an income-generating green energy play. Williams offers steady dividends with ample exposure to the AI boom. Energy stocks can be volatile short-term investments, since commodity prices are cyclical. However, the biggest blue chip energy stocks can still be reliable long-term investments, since their scale insulates them from lower commodity prices. Many of those top energy stocks also return a large share of their excess cash to investors through large dividends. Let's take a look at three of those high-yield energy stocks -- Chevron(NYSE:CVX), Brookfield Renewable(NYSE:BEPC), and The Williams Companies(NYSE:WMB) -- and see why they're worth buying and holding for at least the next ten years. Missed AI’s "Act 1"? Act 2 Could Be 15x Bigger. Most investors think they missed the AI boat because they didn't buy Nvidia in 2005. But according to our analysts, we’re only at the end of "Act 1"—the R&D phase. "Act 2" is the global rollout. Continue » Chevron, one of the world's largest integrated energy companies, pays a forward yield of 3.3%. It's raised its dividend annually for 39 consecutive years, even as the U.S. economy endured three official recessions and five bear markets. Chevron is resilient because it operates in 180 countries and owns a diverse mix of upstream, midstream, and downstream assets. That scale dilutes its operating expenses and allows it to easily cover its capex and dividends as long as the price of Brent crude oil -- currently at $92 -- stays above its corporate breakeven price of $50 per barrel. The last time Brent traded below $50 per barrel was during the darkest days of the COVID-19 pandemic. Chevron expects to increase its oil and gas production by 2%-3% annually through 2030. It plans to hit that target by expanding its Tengiz Field in Kazakhstan, drilling for more oil in the Permian Basin, launching more deepwater projects in the Gulf of Mexico, and increasing its presence in Guyana, one of the world's fastest-growing oil regions. Therefore, Chevron is a great income-generating energy stock you can buy and forget for at least the next 10 years. Brookfield Renewable Corporation, which was spun off from Brookfield Renewable Partners(NYSE:BEP) in 2020, builds hydroelectric dams, wind farms, solar power plants, and other green energy projects across 25 countries. It's raised its dividend every year since that spin-off, and it currently pays a forward dividend yield of 5.1%. With an operational capacity of 51.4 GW and a pipeline of over 200 GW of renewable projects (including 85.7 GW of advanced-stage projects in active development), Brookfield is a great all-around investment in cleaner energy. Roughly 90% of its power generation is locked into long-term contracts with a weighted-average remaining contract duration of 12 years. About 70% of its revenue is also indexed to inflation, which insulates it from rising costs. Brookfield easily covered its dividends with its funds from operations (FFO) last year, and it plans to keep raising its payout by 5%-9% annually. Those strengths make Brookfield a safe green energy play that will continue to generate stable income over the next decade. The Williams Companies operates over 32,000 miles of pipeline in 24 states. It owns Transco, the largest natural gas pipeline in the U.S., which links the Gulf Coast to the Atlantic seaboard. It handles roughly a third of all natural gas produced in the country. Williams is benefiting from the rapid growth of the data center market, which gets more than 40% of its electricity from natural gas, as well as other industrial markets. As a midstream pipeline company, it merely charges upstream and downstream companies "tolls" to use its infrastructure. That business model is well insulated from volatile commodity prices, since it merely needs those resources to keep flowing through its pipes to generate stable profits. Williams has paid continuous dividends for the past 52 years, and it's raised its payout annually over the past nine years. It currently pays a forward yield of 3.1% and offers a good blend of growth and income, with some passive exposure to the booming AI market. title: Is Chevron Stock Increasing Your Market Risk? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Anthropic IPO: Priced For 2031, Or 2036? Investors holding Chevron (CVX) alongside a broader index fund may have noticed the stock moving on its own. Chevron’s share price rose 1.5% from November 10 to November 17, 2026, while the S&P 500 lost 2.4%. A stock that detaches from the index changes how a bad market day affects a portfolio. So when the market falls, does Chevron fall with the rest of your money? On average, no: in the year to November 17, 2026, Chevron tended to move the opposite way to the index. On the average day the S&P 500 fell, a drop of 0.632%, a $10,000 holding in Chevron gained about $58. On the average day the index rose by 0.667%, that same holding lost about $25. Beta measures how far a stock moves for each 1% the index moves. Chevron’s beta was -0.51 over that year. Across all days, the stock tended to move about half as far as the index, in the opposite direction. It fell on the index’s three worst days, though: on November 5, 2026, when the S&P 500 fell 4.4%, Chevron fell 1.9%. It also fell 0.6% on each of the index’s next two worst days. The index fell 2.6% on June 5, 2026, and 2.1% on January 20, 2026. Chevron also exhibited wider swings on its own. The stock’s volatility, a measure of how widely the price swings over a year, was 24.6% over the past year, against 13.8% for the index. Chevron therefore pulled some broader market risk out of a portfolio, but it introduced larger price swings of its own. Chevron’s swings are likely to stay wide, because its earnings move with oil and fuel prices that management calls very volatile. On the October 30, 2026 call, management said oil traded as low as $68 and as high as $132 a barrel within the third quarter. It said adjusted upstream earnings, from producing oil and gas, fell from the second quarter. The causes were lower realized prices, lower volumes sold and unfavorable timing effects. Adjusted downstream earnings rose on higher refining margins. Management also expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term, with 10% of the world’s refining capacity offline. Chevron’s pull against the market is less certain to last. Its correlation with the index, a score from -1 to 1 of how closely two prices move together, was -0.29 over the past year. That figure stood at 0.29 over the five years from November 2021, reflecting a loose tendency to move with the market rather than against it. Yes, by a little. Including dividends, Chevron returned 17.6% a year from November 9, 2021 to November 17, 2026. The S&P 500 returned 10.9% a year over the same dates. Its annual volatility over those five years was 25.4%, against 17.2% for the index. Chevron earned 0.693 of yearly return for each unit of swing, against 0.634 for the index. So Chevron’s swings have paid slightly better than the market’s. Management said Chevron has raised its dividend for 39 consecutive years. Chevron tended to slip slightly on the market’s good days and gain on its bad ones over the past year. Held beside an index fund, the stock has on average offset part of the market’s moves in both directions. It still fell on the index’s three worst days of the year. For investors who already own oil producers, refiners or an energy fund, buying Chevron adds more of that same bet on oil and fuel prices. Chevron’s refining margins are the measure to watch at its next report, expected in January 2027. Chevron’s return over those five years included a dividend that management keeps raising. title: Is Chevron Stock Overpriced Versus Its Oil Rivals? - Trefis

Follow The Cash Chevron (CVX) stock trades at 15.8 times earnings, the second-highest price among six oil companies in its peer group, yet three of them, all refiners, grew sales faster. The price appears to assume that Chevron will keep earning more on its sales than those refiners, and that new oil from Venezuela arrives as planned. So how much more does Chevron actually make on each dollar of sales? Chevron Keeps More Of Each Sales Dollar Than Refiners Chevron kept 14.6% of its revenue as operating profit over the four quarters ended September 30, 2026. Marathon Petroleum (MPC) kept 11.4%. Over the same four quarters, Marathon Petroleum grew revenue 31.2%, compared with 20.8% for Chevron. Yet its shares trade at just 7.7 times earnings. The extra price you pay for Chevron buys a wider margin, not faster growth. Chevron’s margin lead holds against all three refiners and against Exxon Mobil (XOM), the one peer in Chevron’s own industry. Exxon Mobil trades at 17.0 times earnings with a thinner margin, so against Exxon Mobil you pay less for more. ConocoPhillips (COP), an oil and gas producer and the one peer both cheaper and slower growing than Chevron, earned an even wider 24.7% margin across its whole company. Unlike the three refiners, Chevron produces its own oil and gas, and its plan to produce more is on track so far. In fiscal 2025, the Downstream segment, which runs the refineries, brought in $142 billion of revenue. The Upstream segment, which produces the oil and gas, brought in $88.4 billion. Chevron markets all the crude from its three Venezuela joint ventures, sending most of it to U.S. refineries such as Pascagoula and El Segundo. Management plans to double output from those ventures to roughly 600,000 barrels a day by 2031. It puts the total cost below $20 a barrel, counting both capital spending and operating costs. On the October 30, 2026 call, management said the ventures were on track for their year-end goal of around 300,000 barrels a day of gross production, up 20% over the past 12 months. Chevron’s Permian fields also topped 1 million barrels a day of oil and gas combined for a sixth straight quarter, and management plans to hold output above that level. Owning the oil as well as the refineries may be what buyers are paying for, though most of the Venezuela growth is still years away. Over the four quarters ended September 30, 2026, Chevron earned $27.0 billion in profit. It earned $22.0 billion of that total in fiscal Q2 and Q3 2026 alone. In fiscal Q1 2026, it earned just $2.21 billion. Oil traded as low as $68 and as high as $132 a barrel in the third quarter, management said, and it expects refining margins to stay elevated in the short term, with 10% of the world’s refining capacity offline. You pay about twice a refiner’s multiple for Chevron today. If its profit slips back toward its first-quarter level, that premium would buy neither faster growth nor a wider margin. Management guided a dividend of $1.78 a share for fiscal Q4 2026. It calls growing the dividend its first priority, and Chevron has done so for 39 consecutive years. So if you pay Chevron’s premium, you are betting that it keeps its margin ahead of the refiners’ and gets its Venezuela oil flowing. Over the four quarters taken together, Chevron’s margin stayed ahead of the refiners’, though its quarterly margin swung from 6.8% to 21.2%. The Venezuela growth is still mostly a plan. Chevron’s operating margin in its fiscal Q4 2026 report, expected in January 2027, is the number to watch. Neither oil prices nor project dates are in a Chevron holder’s hands. This is a good reason to spread your money across a group of strong companies rather than holding just one. title: Petrobras Stock After Q3 Earnings - Buy, Sell or Hold for Now? - The Globe and Mail
content: Brazil's state-run energy giant Petroleo Brasileiro S.A., better known as PetrobrasPBR, not only produced more oil and gas but also earned more than a year earlier in the third quarter of 2026. It also raised its annual production and cash-flow forecasts. Those are good reasons to look at the stock, even after its sharp rise this year. There are reasons for caution, too, as profit declined from the second quarter, while spending increased. For investors wondering whether to buy, the question is how much of the expected improvement is already priced in. Petrobras reported revenues of $33 billion, up 40.4% from a year earlier. Profit attributable to shareholders rose 28.4% to $7.7 billion. Excluding one-off items, profit increased 78% to $9.3 billion. Operating cash flow reached $12 billion, up 22%, while free cash flow rose 33.2% to $6.6 billion. Free cash flow measures what remains after investment spending. The stock has already rewarded investors. PBR shares have gained 54.8% in 2026 compared with 41.8% for ExxonMobil HoldingsXOM and 44.3% for ChevronCVX. A large gain alone does not tell us whether a stock is expensive, but it makes the earnings outlook worth examining closely. The results were weaker than the second quarter. Reported shareholder profit fell 25.8%, while profit excluding one-off items declined 15.9%. Lower oil prices hurt earnings, as did higher expenses. Investors should keep that comparison in mind when assessing the much stronger annual numbers. Petrobras produced a record 3.512 million barrels of oil equivalent per day (MMBOE/d) during the quarter. Refineries ran at 99% of capacity, and diesel production reached a record 769,000 barrels daily. Management now expects annual production of 3.3–3.4 MMBOE/d, up from 3.1 million. Offshore platforms are reaching higher output sooner, and the P-79 platform started earlier than planned. Petrobras also raised its operating cash-flow forecast to $45-$50 billion from $35 billion. That forecast uses higher production and revised oil-price assumptions, so the increase does not come entirely from operating improvements. ExxonMobil reported production growth in Guyana and the Permian, excluding Middle East effects, while Chevron increased capacity at existing facilities. For Petrobras, the same basic test applies: does spending lead to more production and enough cash to justify the cost? Fourth-quarter production faces scheduled maintenance and a lower Petrobras share of output under the Búzios production-sharing agreement. Investors should not assume production will rise every quarter. The Zacks Consensus Estimate for Petrobras’ 2026 earnings is $4.95 per share, up 76.8% from $2.80 in 2025. That expected increase gives the share-price rally some support. The forecast still depends on production, costs and oil prices, and it should be treated as an expectation rather than money already earned. PBR trades at a lower forward price-to-earnings ratio than its industry, ExxonMobil and Chevron. Put simply, investors pay less for each dollar of Petrobras’ expected earnings. That makes the stock worth considering after its rally. The discount needs context. Petrobras is state-controlled, which creates a risk that government priorities influence business decisions. A cheaper earnings multiple is attractive only if investors are comfortable with those risks and the earnings used to calculate it. Petrobras raised its annual cash investment forecast to $21-$22 billion from $16.9 billion. Its manageable operating expense forecast increased to $24.2–$25.5 billion from $20.2 billion. Management nevertheless expects those expenses per barrel to fall 2% from 2025. Higher lease payments also use cash. Investors comparing Petrobras with ExxonMobil and Chevron should consider how much remains for shareholders after investment and other commitments. Net debt fell to $57.8 billion. Fitch raised Petrobras’ standalone credit profile to bbb+, although its global rating remained BB. The Amapá discovery may offer future resources, but commercial development is uncertain. The agreement to buy the remaining Logum stake also awaits approvals, and its logistics benefits are expected ahead. PBR looks like a buy for investors willing to accept oil-price swings and the risks of state control. Higher production and expected earnings growth support that view, while the valuation remains below peers despite the rally. Rising spending deserves attention because higher operating cash flow does not automatically mean more money for shareholders. On balance, the price and earnings outlook favor buying over selling or waiting. Petrobras stock is currently a Zacks Rank #2 (Buy).
